rows.verified: Hand-arm vibration is a widespread occupational hazard across many industries and occupations.
The Control of Vibration at Work Regulations require employers to manage and control health risks from hand-arm vibration.
Risk assessment should identify workers at risk and the measures needed to reduce exposure.
Where exposure is at or above the exposure action value, employers must implement a planned programme of vibration control.
Alternative processes, mechanisation and automation can eliminate or reduce exposure.
Equipment should be suitable for the task and selected to minimise vibration while completing the work efficiently.
High-vibration tools should be limited where reasonably practicable.
Health surveillance is required for workers regularly exposed above the action value or otherwise considered at risk.
Hand-arm-vibration risk depends on tool vibration magnitude, trigger time, grip, posture, maintenance, temperature, work pattern and individual susceptibility.
HSE vibration evidence is tool-, task-, exposure-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
Employers must protect workers from injury risks arising from hazardous manual handling.
Manual handling includes lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or otherwise moving loads by hand or bodily force.
The first control step is to avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable.
Handling operations that cannot be avoided must be assessed for injury risk.
Identified risks must be reduced to as low as reasonably practicable.
The law does not set a single universal maximum weight limit for manual handling.
Handling aids and task or workplace redesign should be considered before relying on technique alone.
Good handling technique can support risk reduction but is not a substitute for higher-order controls.
Manual-handling risk depends on load, task, posture, frequency, distance, environment, individual capability, aids and work organisation.
HSE manual-handling evidence is load-, task-, worker-, workplace-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
